name: Jebel Irhoud
hook: Skulls once read as Neanderthal; dated in 2017 to ~315,000 years and proposed as earliest H. sapiens.
claim: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud are about 315,000 years old and represent an early stage of the Homo sapiens lineage, placing our species' origin about 100,000 years earlier than accepted and implying the lineage had already spread across Africa rather than arising only in East Africa.

claimed_age.label: 315 ± 34 ka (TL)
claimed_age.basis: Weighted mean TL age of heated flints with the new fossils; U-series/ESR gave 286±32 ka for the Irhoud 3 tooth, a recalculated 1960s find (previously 160±16 ka). Ages predate 1950 measurement; BP offset negligible.

accepted_age.label: ~315,000 years (281–349 ka)
accepted_age.basis: No published re-dating has challenged the 2017 ages. Critics of the H. sapiens attribution, such as Mounier & Mirazón Lahr (2019), use 315 ± 34 ka.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: Homo sapiens emerged about 200,000 years ago in East Africa; the oldest accepted fossil (Omo Kibish, Ethiopia) was ~195,000 years old.

unambiguous_signal.note: Hominin fossils with Middle Stone Age tools are unambiguous. Calling them H. sapiens rests on a mosaic: modern face and teeth, archaic braincase.

documented_context.note: New fossils and dated flints were excavated in place from 2004, with micromorphology. The most complete skull, Irhoud 1, was a 1961 mining find.

multiple_dating_methods.note: TL on heated flints (315±34 ka) and recalculated U-series/ESR on the Irhoud 3 tooth (286±32 ka) broadly agreed; fauna and microfauna were consistent. Overlap with TL's dose-rate data: UNVERIFIED.

multiple_labs.note: TL was run by D. Richter (Max Planck, Leipzig); ESR by R. Grün and R. Joannes-Boyau (Griffith, ANU and Southern Cross universities, Australia).

professional_recovery.note: New fossils were found in place during excavations by a Moroccan INSAP and Max Planck team, begun in 2004.

peer_reviewed_report.note: Two papers in Nature, June 2017; named reviewers included R. G. Klein and C. Stringer.

material_accessible.note: An independent team re-analysed Irhoud 1 morphologically (Mounier & Mirazón Lahr 2019); specimen access (cast vs. original) unconfirmed. No independent study of new originals within five years found.

independent_teams.note: Fossils and dates came from one INSAP–Max Planck project. The only independent re-analysis within five years (S9, 2019) disagreed with the H. sapiens attribution.

proponent_stake.note: Academic project of INSAP and the Max Planck Institute; authors declared no competing financial interests. No outside motive documented.

objections.text: The long, low braincase and the face shape suggest a more primitive ancestor, a snapshot from just before modern humans evolved, rather than H. sapiens.
objections.outcome_note: Proponents argue brain shape evolved gradually within the lineage (Neubauer et al. 2018). Where to draw the species line is still debated.

objections.text: Membership depends on the defining traits: if a globular skull defines H. sapiens, the Irhoud people are close cousins, not members of our species.
objections.outcome_note: Scerri et al. (2018) include Irhoud in the H. sapiens clade. Vidal et al. (2022) note most late Middle Pleistocene candidates have uncertain ages or debatable H. sapiens traits generally, not specific to Irhoud.

objections.text: The team did not compare Irhoud with Homo antecessor; its modern-looking face might be retained from an older, antecessor-like ancestor.
objections.outcome_note: No study directly compares Irhoud with H. antecessor. Hublin's team's 2026 Casablanca-fossil study (S15) argues an African lineage ancestral to H. sapiens, distinct from antecessor — the proponents' answer, unresolved.

objections.text: Irhoud 1's overall skull shape is closest to Neanderthals; North Africans may be a side population that mixed into Neanderthals, with H. sapiens arising further south and east.
objections.outcome_note: The same group repeated the view in 2023 (S14); the proponents still call Irhoud the earliest H. sapiens (S15, 2026).

status_note: Open: the ~315 ka age is accepted, but whether the fossils are early H. sapiens is contested. The only independent re-analyses (2019, 2023) place them nearer Neanderthals; the proponents (2018, 2026) keep the attribution.

timeline.event: Workmen at a barite mine find a hominin skull, later called Irhoud 1.
Émile Ennouchi describes Irhoud 1 as a Neanderthal.
Hublin finds no Neanderthal traits and clear shared derived traits with modern humans; ESR suggests an older age (isotope stage 5 or 6).
A Moroccan (INSAP) and Max Planck team begins new excavations.
U-series/ESR dates the Irhoud 3 juvenile jaw to 160 ± 16 ka; it is called early Homo sapiens.
Two Nature papers report new fossils and a TL age of 315 ± 34 ka, and call Irhoud an early stage of the H. sapiens clade.
John Hawks and Marta Mirazón Lahr question whether the fossils belong to H. sapiens.
Ancient genomes put the first split among modern human populations at 350,000–260,000 years ago.
A 23-author synthesis calls Irhoud the oldest currently recognized members of the H. sapiens clade.
Mounier and Mirazón Lahr find Irhoud 1 closer to Neanderthals in overall shape and judge a North African origin less likely.
Omo I in Ethiopia is redated to at least 233 ± 22 ka.
Hublin's team describes ~773 ka Casablanca fossils as basal to the H. sapiens lineage, again calling Irhoud the earliest H. sapiens.

decisive_tests.test: Attempt enamel protein sequencing on an Irhoud tooth, as done for Homo antecessor (Welker et al. 2020), to help place Irhoud relative to Neanderthals and H. sapiens.
decisive_tests.would_show: May help indicate whether Irhoud sits nearer H. sapiens or Neanderthals; proteomes may carry too few informative sites among close Middle Pleistocene Homo to be conclusive.

decisive_tests.test: Re-date archived heated flints or sediment from the fossil layer at a second, independent luminescence laboratory.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the ~315 ka age reproduces outside the original team's laboratories.

decisive_tests.test: Directly date the newly excavated in-situ fossil teeth (e.g. Irhoud 10/11) by U-series/ESR at a second, independent laboratory.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the only direct fossil age (286 ka, a recalculation of a 1960s find) reproduces on material excavated and dated as a unit.

falsifier: Toward refuted: re-dating the fossil layer well below ~250 ka, or protein or fuller morphological evidence placing Irhoud outside the H. sapiens lineage (e.g. nearer Neanderthals). Toward vindicated: such evidence placing it within the H. sapiens clade.

confidence_note: Facts are well sourced. 'Open' reflects a live taxonomic dispute; the 286 ka ESR date's independence from TL dose-rate data is unverified. S2 read via abstract only.
corrections: Brief: fossils 'long treated as Neanderthal-like' until 2017. Actually Hublin (1992) rejected that reading, and Smith et al. (2007) already called Irhoud 'early Homo sapiens' at ~160 ka; 2017's novelty was the age.

Brief: the 2017 papers 'dated them to ~300,000 years (thermoluminescence on heated flints)'. TL dated the flints, not the fossils; the only direct fossil date (U-series/ESR, 286±32 ka) recalculates a 1960s find once dated 160±16 ka.

Brief's 'Expected status: vindicated' overstates consensus: the brief and common accounts call Irhoud simply the oldest H. sapiens, but the only independent re-analyses (S9, S14) dispute the species attribution; recorded as open.
notes: The claim coded here is the 2017 one; finds date from 1961. Earlier ages: ~40 ka (S7), then ESR 130–190 ka (Grün & Stringer 1991, per S9), then 160 ± 16 ka (S4). A pan-African origin (S10; cf. S17, no single birthplace) is debated (S9). Omo I was later redated to at least 233 ka (S12), narrowing the leap. Mundane checks: no published challenge to the dates, association or specimen integrity was found; whether the recalculated 286 ka ESR/U-series date shares dose-rate inputs with the TL work is UNVERIFIED; a 2018 correction (S16) fixed figure labels and sample counts without changing conclusions. The live dispute is taxonomic, not chronological.

open_issues: Plates removed: Commons lists CC BY 4.0 for both MPI EVA photos, but the archived 2017 press kit labels both CC-BY-SA 2.0 (matching credits: Schatz; Kamal). Unresolved without a Commons correction, so no plates are recorded.
D19 re-rating 2026-09-23: partial → open — no part of the core claim failed: the ~315 ka age is accepted, while H. sapiens membership is actively contested by independent re-analyses (2019, 2023).
